**The Weight of a Name**

There was a time when names were not just labels, but promises. My mother’s name, *Lila*, meant "play" in Sanskrit, but she never played—she worked. My father’s name, *Raj*, meant "king," but he was a man who bowed to the weight of his own hands, who knew the difference between a crown and a callous. I was named *Anika*, which means "without sin," but I have spent my life trying to understand what that could possibly mean.

I was twelve when I first heard the word *refugee* spoken aloud in our home. It was not a word we used. We were *displaced*. We were *temporary*. We were *waiting*. But the word *refugee* carried a weight, a history, a story that made my chest tighten. It was the sound of a door closing behind us, not just in the physical sense, but in the way people looked at us—like we were already ghosts, already fading.

My father had a habit of collecting things. Coins from every country we lived in. Stamps. Small trinkets from markets. Once, when I was eight, I found a stack of old newspapers in his desk. They were yellowed, brittle. I didn’t understand them at first, but then I saw the headlines: *Massacre in Darfur*, *Floods Devastate Bangladesh*, *War Crimes Trial Begins*. My father had been reading them for years. He never spoke of them, but he saved them like they were relics, like they were proof that the world was still turning, even when it felt like it wasn’t.

I remember the first time I saw snow. We had moved to a city where the air was so cold it burned your lungs. The ground was white, untouched, and for a moment, I thought it was magic. My father had told me stories of snow when I was small—how it fell like God’s own confetti, how it could silence the world. But standing there, watching the flakes drift down, I realized that snow was not magic. It was just another kind of displacement. It covered the ground, but it didn’t erase the cracks. It didn’t make the cold any less real.

I was sixteen when I first left the house without my father’s permission. I didn’t steal. I didn’t lie. I just walked out the door and didn’t come back until the sun was setting. My mother found me at the bus station, her face pale. "Where do you think you’re going?" she asked, her voice trembling. I told her I didn’t know. I just needed to see something—anything—that wasn’t our apartment, our street, our life.

She didn’t scold me. She just took my hand and led me to the park. We sat on a bench, and she told me about the time she was twelve and ran away to the beach. She said she wanted to see the ocean, but all she saw was the sky and the sand and the way the wind could make you feel like you were flying. "Names don’t matter," she said. "What matters is where you go."

I didn’t believe her then. But I believe it now.

I am twenty-five now, and I have a name that means "without sin," but I have made mistakes. I have loved too hard and too little. I have been kind when I should have been cruel, and cruel when I should have been kind. I have been a refugee in my own life, moving from one city to another, from one job to another, always searching for something that doesn’t exist.

But I have also found things. I found a book in a secondhand store that belonged to my father. It was a collection of poems by a woman named *Meena*, who wrote about the weight of memory and the way time could bend like a river. I read it in one sitting, and for the first time, I understood what my father had been trying to tell me all along. Names are not just words. They are echoes. They are the voices of those who came before us, whispering through the years.

I am not a refugee anymore. I am just a woman who has lived in too many places and loved too many people and lost too many things. But I am still searching. I am still trying to understand what it means to be *without sin*, to be *play*, to be *king*. Maybe it means knowing that you are not alone. Maybe it means knowing that the world is still turning, even when it feels like it isn’t.

I am sitting in a café now, writing this in a notebook that cost me five dollars. The coffee is bitter, the air is thick with the hum of conversation, and outside, the city is alive. I am not a ghost. I am not fading. I am just here, in this moment, trying to make sense of it all.

And maybe, just maybe, that’s enough.
